title: Lecture #9: Introduction to Arrays
topics: Array declaration and creation with new

questions.topic: Array declaration and creation with new
questions.question: In `int[] rollNums = new int[3];`, what do the keyword `new` and the number `3` do, according to the lecture?
options: `new` copies an existing array, and 3 is the value stored in every element
`new` allocates memory for the array in the heap, and 3 is the size (number of int elements)
`new` declares the variable name, and 3 is the last valid index
`new` is optional decoration, and 3 is the number of dimensions
questions.explanation: The notes label `int[]` as the data type, `rollNums` as the identifier, `new` as the special keyword that allocates memory in the heap, and `[3]` as the size, giving room for three 32-bit ints. With size 3 the last valid index is 2, not 3.

questions.question: Following the String example from the lecture, what does this snippet print?
options: Aditya Tandon
fname + lname
A compile error, because + only works on numbers
AdityaTandon
questions.explanation: `+` between two Strings joins them exactly as they are, and neither String contains a space, so the result is AdityaTandon. That is why the lecture's Demo3.java builds the full name as `firstName + " " + lastName`, adding the space explicitly.

questions.question: `rollNums` was created with `new int[3]` and holds 101, 102, 103. A teammate writes `System.out.println(rollNums[3]);` to print the last roll number. What happens?
options: It compiles, but at runtime it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2
It prints 103, because index 3 means the third element
It prints 0, the default value for a missing element
It does not compile, because the compiler checks every index
questions.explanation: Indexing starts at 0, so the third element (103) is at rollNums[2]; index 3 lies outside the array, which the JVM detects at runtime (the notes' 'index out of bound exception'). The compiler does not check index values, so it is not a compile error.

questions.question: How does the lecture describe a 2-D array such as `int[][] marks` in Java?
options: A single block of memory that can only be read row by row
Two separate arrays that must always have the same length
An array of arrays: each element of `marks` is itself a 1-D int array (a row)
A special String table with rows and columns
questions.explanation: The notes draw `marks` as a 1-D array whose slots point to row arrays (marks[0], marks[1], marks[2]); a 1-D array is an 'array of int' and a 2-D array is an 'array of arrays'. Because each row is its own array, rows do not have to be the same length.

questions.question: This is based on the lecture's Demo.java. What does it print?
questions.explanation: The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2 (`length` is 3), storing 101, 102, 103; x is incremented after each store, so it ends at 104 (the notes track x going 101 -> 102 -> 103 -> 104). `length` is the number of elements (3), not the last index (2).

questions.question: The lecture stores students' marks in `int[][] marks = new int[3][3];` with rows S1, S2, S3 and columns Hindi, English, CSE: S1 = 50 30 90, S2 = 60 40 80, S3 = 70 50 70. Which expression gives S3's English mark?
options: marks[3][2]
marks[1][2]
marks[2][2]
marks[2][1]
questions.explanation: The first index is the row (student) and the second the column (subject), both starting at 0: S3 is row 2 and English is column 1, so marks[2][1] = 50. marks[3][2] uses 1-based counting and would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; marks[2][2] is S3's CSE mark (70).

questions.question: A teammate builds the jagged array `int[][] marks = new int[3][];` with `marks[0] = new int[2]; marks[1] = new int[3]; marks[2] = new int[4];` and prints it using `for (int col = 0; col < 3; col++)` inside the row loop. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing; Java pads short rows with zeros so a fixed 3 works for every row
It does not compile, because rows of different lengths are not allowed
Row 0 has only 2 columns, so col = 2 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; use `col < marks[row].length` (and row 2's 4th value would be skipped anyway)
Only the last row is printed; the fix is `row <= marks.length`
questions.explanation: In a jagged array every row is a separate array with its own length, so the inner loop must use `marks[row].length`, exactly as the lecture's improved loop does; a hard-coded 3 overruns row 0 and under-reads row 2. Java does not pad rows, and `row <= marks.length` would itself go out of bounds.

questions.question: A teammate coming from C wants an int array holding 4, 5 and 6, and tries several lines. Which one compiles in Java?
questions.explanation: The shortcut initializer from the notes (`int[] rollNums = {4, 5, 6};`) is allowed in the declaration itself, and the size is taken from the number of values. A bare `{...}` cannot be assigned later, you cannot give both a size and an initializer list, and Java never puts the size in the declaration as C does.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: marks.length is the number of rows (3) and marks[2].length is the length of the last row (3), not the total element count 6. The stored values are row 0: 0; row 1: 1, 2; row 2: 2, 3, 4, which sum to 0 + 3 + 9 = 12.

questions.question: For the lecture's 3-D array `int[][][] arr = new int[3][3][3];`, what exactly is `arr[0][0]`?
options: A single int value
A 2-D array (3 x 3) of ints
A 1-D array of 3 ints, e.g. the notes' {3, 4, 7}
The total element count, 27
questions.explanation: Each index peels off one dimension: arr is an array of three 2-D arrays, arr[0] is one 2-D array (3 x 3), and arr[0][0] is one of its rows, a 1-D int array of length 3; only arr[0][0][0] is a single int. The notes draw exactly this, with arr[0][0] pointing at a row holding 3, 4, 7.
